claim: During mitosis, individual microtubules make attachments to chromosomes via a specialized protein complex called the kinetochore to faithfully segregate the chromosomes to daughter cells.
source: During mitosis, individual microtubules make attachments to chromosomes via a specialized protein complex called the kinetochore to faithfully segregate the chromosomes to daughter cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: Translocation of kinetochores on the lateral surface of the microtubule has been proposed to contribute to high fidelity chromosome capture and alignment at the mitotic midzone.
source: Translocation of kinetochores on the lateral surface of the microtubule has been proposed to contribute to high fidelity chromosome capture and alignment at the mitotic midzone, but has been difficult to observe in vivo because of spatial and temporal constraints.
evidence: This claim references prior proposals in the field about kinetochore translocation mechanisms.

claim: TIRF microscopy and cryo-correlative light microscopy and electron tomography indicated successful reconstitution of interactions between intact kinetochores and microtubules.
source: TIRF microscopy and cryo-correlative light microscopy and electron tomography indicated that we successfully reconstituted interactions between intact kinetochores and microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple microscopy techniques presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reconstituted kinetochores translocate on the lateral microtubule surface toward the microtubule plus end.
source: These kinetochores translocate on the lateral microtubule surface toward the microtubule plus end and transition to end-on attachment, whereupon microtubule depolymerization commences.
evidence: This is directly observed in the TIRF microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kinetochores transition from lateral to end-on attachment at the microtubule plus end.
source: These kinetochores translocate on the lateral microtubule surface toward the microtubule plus end and transition to end-on attachment, whereupon microtubule depolymerization commences.
evidence: This transition is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Microtubule depolymerization commences after kinetochores transition to end-on attachment.
source: These kinetochores translocate on the lateral microtubule surface toward the microtubule plus end and transition to end-on attachment, whereupon microtubule depolymerization commences.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and kymographs in Figure 1.

claim: The directional kinetochore movement is dependent on the highly processive kinesin-8, Kip3.
source: The directional kinetochore movement is dependent on the highly processive kinesin-8, Kip3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with kip3Δ mutants shown in Figure 4.

claim: Kip3 facilitates stable kinetochore attachment to microtubule plus ends through its ability to move the kinetochore laterally on the surface of the microtubule.
source: We propose that Kip3 facilitates stable kinetochore attachment to microtubule plus ends through its abilities to move the kinetochore laterally on the surface of the microtubule and to regulate microtubule plus end dynamics.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations with Kip3 mutants.

claim: Kip3 facilitates stable kinetochore attachment to microtubule plus ends through its ability to regulate microtubule plus end dynamics.
source: We propose that Kip3 facilitates stable kinetochore attachment to microtubule plus ends through its abilities to move the kinetochore laterally on the surface of the microtubule and to regulate microtubule plus end dynamics.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations of microtubule dynamics in different Kip3 conditions.

claim: Proper kinetochore-microtubule attachment is vital for preservation of genomic integrity and prevention of cancer and birth defects.
source: Proper kinetochore-microtubule attachment is vital for preservation of genomic integrity and prevention of cancer and birth defects (Weaver and Cleveland, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Kinetochore attachment is highly regulated and tightly controlled.
source: Therefore, kinetochore attachment is highly regulated and tightly controlled (Tanaka, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: During establishment of biorientation, kinetochores have been observed to first attach to the lateral surface of a microtubule.
source: During establishment of biorientation, kinetochores have been observed to first attach to the lateral surface of a microtubule (Tanaka, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Laterally bound kinetochores must be transported along the microtubule lattice where they transition to an appropriate, and stable, end-on attachment.
source: Such kinetochores then must be transported along the microtubule lattice, where they transition to an appropriate, and stable, end-on attachment (Rieder and Alexander, 1990; Tanaka et al., 2005a; Kapoor et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cell will progress into anaphase and complete mitosis only after each sister kinetochore makes a proper end-on attachment with microtubules from opposite spindle poles.
source: It is only after each sister kinetochore makes a proper end-on attachment with microtubules from opposite spindle poles that the cell will progress into anaphase and complete mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Lateral to end-on attachment conversion has been observed in several eukaryotic species.
source: This lateral to end-on attachment conversion has been observed in several eukaryotic species (Magidson et al., 2015; Maiato et al., 2017), but the underlying mechanisms have been elusive due both to the difficulty of observing this event in vivo and to biochemical hurdles in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CENP-E and chromokinesins are particularly important for chromosome movement to the spindle midzone in metazoans.
source: With regard to the kinetochore reaching the microtubule tip, CENP-E and chromokinesins are particularly important for chromosome movement to the spindle midzone in metazoans (Craske and Welburn, 2020; Lemura and Tanaka, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fungi do not appear to have kinesin-7 or chromokinesin orthologs.
source: However, fungi do not appear to have kinesin-7 or chromokinesin orthologs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of fungal genomes.

claim: Lateral to end-on conversion has been observed in fungi, but these events required that a depolymerizing microtubule tip meet the laterally bound kinetochore.
source: Lateral to end-on conversion has been observed in fungi, but these events required that a depolymerizing microtubule tip meet the laterally bound kinetochore (Kalantzaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Other studies in fungi have implicated minus-end directed motor-based transport of unattached kinetochores.
source: Other studies in fungi have also implicated minus-end directed motor-based transport of unattached kinetochores (Tanaka et al., 2005a), similar to a proposed metazoan mechanism involving the motor protein dynein and the mitotic spindle protein NuMA (Kapoor et al., 2006; Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kinesin-8 proteins have been proposed to tune microtubule dynamics for proper chromosome segregation through a dual-mode mechanism of destabilizing growing microtubules and stabilizing depolymerizing microtubules.
source: Through a dual-mode mechanism of destabilizing growing microtubules and stabilizing depolymerizing microtubules, kinesin-8 proteins have been proposed to tune microtubule dynamics for proper chromosome segregation (Risteski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In budding yeast, Kip3 is required for kinetochore clustering into two discrete foci at metaphase.
source: In budding yeast, Kip3, a highly processive kinesin-8, is required for kinetochore clustering into two discrete foci at metaphase, but how this activity relates to establishment of end-on attachments is not clear (Wargacki et al., 2010; Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Declustered kinetochores may represent misaligned or defectively attached chromosomes.
source: Declustered kinetochores may represent misaligned or defectively attached chromosomes (Wargacki et al., 2010; Edzuka and Goshima, 2019; Shimogawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In yeast that lack Kip3, chromosomes lag behind the main chromosome mass during anaphase.
source: Additionally, in yeast that lack Kip3, chromosomes lag behind the main chromosome mass during anaphase (Tytell and Sorger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The metazoan kinesin-8, Kif18a, is responsible for tuning kinetochore-microtubule dynamics, which ultimately affects chromosome alignment and equal segregation into the daughter cells.
source: The metazoan kinesin-8, Kif18a, is responsible for tuning kinetochore-microtubule dynamics, which ultimately affects chromosome alignment and equal segregation into the daughter cells (Stumpff et al., 2008; Stumpff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lagging chromosomes are common in cells lacking Kif18a and result in micronuclei formation.
source: Lagging chromosomes are common in cells lacking Kif18a and result in micronuclei formation (Fonseca et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Drosophila kinesin-8, Klp67A, shares many of the roles of other kinesin-8 proteins including stabilizing and destabilizing microtubules.
source: Additionally, the Drosophila kinesin-8, Klp67A, shares many of the roles of other kinesin-8 proteins including stabilizing and destabilizing microtubules, but this kinesin also stabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Edzuka and Goshima, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Drosophila kinesin-8, Klp67A, stabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
source: Additionally, the Drosophila kinesin-8, Klp67A, shares many of the roles of other kinesin-8 proteins including stabilizing and destabilizing microtubules, but this kinesin also stabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Edzuka and Goshima, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Kinesin-8 motor proteins have roles both in regulating microtubule dynamics and in establishing kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that kinesin-8 motor proteins have roles both in regulating microtubule dynamics and in establishing kinetochore-microtubule attachments, while potentially playing a role in the formation of proper end-on attachments.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and observations.

claim: Ndc80 and Ask1 kinetochore signals appeared on the microtubule surface and moved processively at an average rate of 0.56 µm/min toward the plus end of the microtubule.
source: Ndc80 and Ask1 kinetochore signals appeared on the microtubule surface (Figure 1c) and moved processively at an average rate of 0.56 µm/min toward the plus end of the microtubule (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: Upon reaching the tip of the microtubule, Ndc80 and Ask1 appeared to transition irreversibly from lateral to end-on attachment.
source: Upon reaching the tip of the microtubule, Ndc80 and Ask1 appeared to transition irreversibly from lateral to end-on attachment.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: End-on binding of Ndc80 and Ask1 was followed by microtubule depolymerization where they tracked the depolymerizing microtubule end.
source: This end-on binding was then followed by microtubule depolymerization where Ndc80 and Ask1 tracked the depolymerizing microtubule end.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mean microtubule depolymerization rate slowed from 0.82 µm/min to an average of 0.4 µm/min upon kinetochore binding to the microtubule tip.
source: The mean microtubule depolymerization rate also slowed from 0.82 µm/min (Bergman et al., 2018) to an average of 0.4 µm/min upon kinetochore binding to the microtubule tip (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is measured from experimental data and compared to a prior study.

claim: After depolymerization onset, the microtubule was never observed to resume growth.
source: After depolymerization onset, the microtubule was never observed to resume growth.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Kinetochore proteins rarely, if ever, detached from the microtubule, either while bound laterally or to the microtubule tip.
source: Additionally, kinetochore proteins rarely, if ever, detached from the microtubule, either while bound laterally or to the microtubule tip.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: While laterally bound, kinetochores only move towards the plus end of the microtubule.
source: While laterally bound, kinetochores only move towards the plus end of the microtubule.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: When the kinetochore transitions from lateral to end-on attachment, the kinetochore only tracks the depolymerizing end of the microtubule and thus moves toward the minus-end of the microtubule.
source: When the kinetochore transitions from lateral to end-on attachment, the kinetochore only tracks the depolymerizing end of the microtubule and thus moves toward the minus-end of the microtubule.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Seven middle and inner kinetochore proteins (Spc105, Mtw1, Cnn1, Okp1, Mif2, Ctf3, and Cse4) have no known microtubule binding capabilities.
source: Overall, these seven middle and inner kinetochore proteins have no known microtubule binding capabilities, implying that the kinetochore signals that we observed might represent intact or nearly intact kinetochores on microtubules in our assay.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of these proteins' functions.

claim: The kinetochore signals observed represent intact or nearly intact kinetochores on microtubules.
source: Overall, these seven middle and inner kinetochore proteins have no known microtubule binding capabilities, implying that the kinetochore signals that we observed might represent intact or nearly intact kinetochores on microtubules in our assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteins without microtubule-binding capability are moving on microtubules.

claim: Mif2 and Cse4 moved at only 67–75% of the velocity of other kinetochore proteins on the microtubule lattice.
source: Two proteins, Mif2 and Cse4, moved at only 67–75% of the velocity of the others on the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mif2 and Cse4 colocalize with other kinetochore proteins in lysate from dual-labeled strains.
source: One possible explanation for the slower velocities of these two proteins is that their GFP protein tags might affect their function; but since these two proteins colocalize with other kinetochore proteins in lysate from dual-labeled strains (Figure 2), we conclude that all the proteins examined are present in common complexes.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All the kinetochore proteins examined are present in common complexes.
source: One possible explanation for the slower velocities of these two proteins is that their GFP protein tags might affect their function; but since these two proteins colocalize with other kinetochore proteins in lysate from dual-labeled strains (Figure 2), we conclude that all the proteins examined are present in common complexes.
evidence: This is concluded from the colocalization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The kinetochore protein dynamics observed in metaphase-arrested cell lysates were specific to metaphase.
source: Importantly, the kinetochore protein dynamics observed in metaphase-arrested cell lysates were specific to metaphase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing metaphase, S-phase, and anaphase lysates in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When Spc105 dynamics were assayed in S-phase or anaphase arrested extracts, the kinetochore proteins were stationary and did not move on the microtubule lattice.
source: When Spc105 dynamics were assayed in S-phase (cdc7-1) or anaphase (cdc15-2) arrested extracts (Goranov et al., 2009), the kinetochore proteins were stationary and did not move on the microtubule lattice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When Spc105 was observed at the microtubule tip in S-phase or anaphase arrested extracts, no tip-associated microtubule depolymerization occurred.
source: Additionally, when Spc105 was observed at the microtubule tip, no tip-associated microtubule depolymerization occurred.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data from S-phase and anaphase lysates.

claim: Colocalization of kinetochore proteins occurred independent of that kinetochore protein's proximity to Ndc80 within the kinetochore.
source: On the contrary, when imaging different kinetochore proteins together with Ndc80, we, in fact, saw colocalization independent of that kinetochore protein's proximity to Ndc80 within the kinetochore (Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When using Mtw1 as a fiducial marker, colocalization between kinetochore proteins was still observed.
source: Additionally, when using Mtw1, a more 'central' kinetochore protein, as a fiducial marker, we still observed colocalization between kinetochore proteins (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The characterized movements of single tagged kinetochore proteins in this assay likely represents entire kinetochore complexes.
source: These data indicate that the characterized movements of single tagged kinetochore proteins in this assay likely represents entire kinetochore complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The mScarlet-I fluorophore used to tag proteins blinked on and off.
source: In our assay, the mScarlet-I fluorophore used to tag proteins blinked on and off (Klementieva et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Other red fluorescent protein tags tested, including mScarlet, TagRFP-T, and mRuby2, also blinked and/or bleached rapidly.
source: Other red fluorescent protein tags tested, including mScarlet, TagRFP-T, and mRuby2, also blinked and/or bleached rapidly.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Ndc80 and Mtw1 never disassociated from microtubules to which they were bound.
source: From our single protein tagging (with GFP) experiments (Figure 1), we knew that Ndc80 and Mtw1 never disassociated from microtubules to which they were bound.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Large protein complexes associated with the lateral surface and the tip of individual microtubules were clearly visible in tomograms.
source: Large protein complexes associated with the lateral surface and the tip of individual microtubules were clearly visible in tomograms of these regions (Figure 3—video 1, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The approximately 100 nm long complexes observed in tomograms are reminiscent of kinetochore particles assembled from purified yeast components.
source: These approximately 100 nm long complexes are reminiscent of kinetochore particles assembled from purified yeast components (Gonen et al., 2012; Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the observed structures to previously published structures.

claim: The tomography data revealed electron densities that likely correspond to the Dam1 ring and the Ndc80 and MIND sub-complexes.
source: Furthermore, our tomography data revealed electron densities that likely correspond to the Dam1 ring and the Ndc80 and MIND sub-complexes (Westermann et al., 2005; Jenni and Harrison, 2018; Ng et al., 2019; Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is inferred from the tomography data by comparing to known structures from the literature.

claim: Multi-protein kinetochore particles were present on yeast microtubules in the reconstitution cell lysate assays.
source: In combination with the co-localization data from the TIRF assay, our tomography data reinforces the conclusion that multi-protein kinetochore particles were present on yeast microtubules in our reconstitution cell lysate assays.
evidence: This is concluded from combining the TIRF colocalization data and the cryo-ET data.

claim: Only the highly processive plus-end directed kinesin-8, Kip3, was necessary for plus-end directed motility of the kinetochores.
source: Upon deleting the genes encoding each of these motors, we found that only the highly processive plus-end directed kinesin-8, Kip3, was necessary for plus-end directed motility of the kinetochores (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by systematic deletion of each kinesin gene shown in Figure 4.

claim: 77% of laterally bound kinetochores moved in Kip3+ lysates compared to only 28% in kip3Δ lysates.
source: Specifically, 77% of laterally bound kinetochores moved in Kip3 +lysates compared to only 28% in kip3Δ lysates.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Laterally bound kinetochores that did move in kip3Δ lysates spent significantly less time moving toward the microtubule plus end compared to wild-type.
source: Moreover, those laterally bound kinetochores that did move in kip3Δ lysates spent significantly less time moving toward the microtubule plus end compared to wild-type, and their run lengths were about half as far as those in Kip3 +lysates (0.46 µm vs 0.73 µm; Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Run lengths of kinetochores in kip3Δ lysates were about half as far as those in Kip3+ lysates (0.46 µm vs 0.73 µm).
source: Moreover, those laterally bound kinetochores that did move in kip3Δ lysates spent significantly less time moving toward the microtubule plus end compared to wild-type, and their run lengths were about half as far as those in Kip3 +lysates (0.46 µm vs 0.73 µm; Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Kinetochore movements in kip3Δ lysates had the same velocity as the movements observed in Kip3+ lysates, moving at 0.47 µm/min.
source: Interestingly, although less frequent and covering shorter distances, kinetochore movements in kip3Δ lysates had the same velocity as the more frequent and longer movements observed in Kip3 +lysates, moving at 0.47 µm/min (Figure 4d; see Discussion).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Only 5.7% of laterally bound kinetochores reached the plus end in kip3Δ lysates, compared to 28.1% in Kip3+ lysates.
source: Because the kinetochore movements in the kip3Δ lysate were relatively infrequent and covered short distances, only 5.7% of laterally bound kinetochores reached the plus end, compared to 28.1% in Kip3 +lysates.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data.

claim: When the kinetochore in the kip3Δ lysates was bound to the tip of the microtubule, depolymerization with the kinetochore tracking the microtubule plus end did occur.
source: As in the Kip3 +lysates, when the kinetochore in the kip3Δ lysates was bound to the tip of the microtubule, depolymerization with the kinetochore tracking the microtubule plus end did occur.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data from kip3Δ lysates.

claim: In kip3Δ lysates, the microtubule plus ends with tip-bound kinetochores spent a significantly lower percentage of the time depolymerizing compared to Kip3+ lysates.
source: However, in this kip3Δ case, the microtubule plus ends with tip-bound kinetochores spent a significantly lower percentage of the time depolymerizing compared to what we observed in Kip3 +lysates (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: This observation is consistent with a role for Kip3 in kinetochore-induced microtubule depolymerization.
source: This observation is consistent with a role for Kip3 in kinetochore-induced microtubule depolymerization (Gupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation and supported by a citation.

claim: 53.7% of the 54 immobile, laterally bound kinetochores in the kip3Δ lysates became motile after Kip3+ lysate was added.
source: Specifically, 53.7% of the 54 immobile, laterally bound kinetochores in the kip3Δ lysates became motile after Kip3 +lysate was added.
evidence: This is quantified from the sequential lysate flow experiment shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Kinetochores assembled in the absence of Kip3 were able to bind to microtubules, but required the subsequent addition of Kip3 and/or its other binding partners to translocate along the lateral surface of microtubules.
source: Therefore, kinetochores assembled in the absence of Kip3 were able to bind to microtubules, but required the subsequent addition of Kip3 and/or its other binding partners to translocate along the lateral surface of microtubules.
evidence: This is concluded from the sequential lysate flow experiment shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Cin8 and Kip1 were observed coming on and off the microtubule lattice stochastically at a high frequency, but they were not motile in the assay.
source: We observed Cin8 and Kip1 coming on and off the microtubule lattice stochastically at a high frequency, but they were not motile in our assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Kar3 was rarely observed on the microtubule.
source: Kar3 was rarely observed on the microtubule (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Only Kip3 and Kip2 moved processively on the microtubule lattice.
source: Of all the motors assayed, only Kip3 and Kip2 moved processively on the microtubule lattice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Kinetochore motility was only disrupted in kip3Δ lysates, not in kip2Δ lysates.
source: However, kinetochore motility was only disrupted in kip3Δ lysates, not in kip2Δ lysates (Figure 4a–d).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4a-d.

claim: Processive motor movement towards the plus end alone is not sufficient to facilitate kinetochore movement along a microtubule.
source: Therefore, processive motor movement towards the plus end alone is not sufficient to facilitate kinetochore movement along a microtubule.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Kip2 is processive but does not facilitate kinetochore movement.

claim: Kinetochore plus-end directed movement is dependent on Kip3 activity specifically.
source: Kinetochore plus-end directed movement is dependent on Kip3 activity specifically.
evidence: This is concluded from the motor deletion experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neither Kip3 nor Kip2 showed persistent colocalization with the kinetochores.
source: However, neither motor showed persistent colocalization with the kinetochores.
evidence: This is observed in the dual-color imaging experiments.

claim: There were brief moments of kinetochore movement where Kip3 signal was observed running over or through the kinetochore signal.
source: The dual color tagging of Kip3 and Spc105 showed that there were brief moments of kinetochore movement where Kip3 signal was observed running over or through the kinetochore signal (Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is observed in the dual-color imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Kip3 moved much faster than either the speed of the kinetochore or the polymerization of the microtubule.
source: Kip3 also moved much faster than either the speed of the kinetochore or the polymerization of the microtubule.
evidence: This is observed in the dual-color imaging experiments.

claim: Knocking out the gene encoding Kip3 results in metaphase kinetochores that stay along the axis of the spindle, but are no longer focused into two discrete foci.
source: In cells, knocking out the gene encoding Kip3 results in metaphase kinetochores that stay along the axis of the spindle, but are no longer focused into two discrete foci (Figure 5a–b; Tytell and Sorger, 2006; Wargacki et al., 2010; Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in the in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5a-b and supported by citations.

claim: The declustered kinetochore phenotype has been proposed to be a result of improper spindle assembly and/or defective kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
source: This declustered kinetochore phenotype has been proposed to be a result of improper spindle assembly and/or defective kinetochore-microtubule attachment (Shimogawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Kip3ΔT-LZ shows a declustered kinetochore phenotype in vivo.
source: Of interest to us was a Kip3 mutant, Kip3ΔT-LZ, that shows a declustered kinetochore phenotype in vivo (Figure 5a–b; Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in the in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5a-b and supported by a citation.

claim: In Kip3ΔT-LZ, the putative cargo-binding tail was truncated and replaced with a leucine zipper domain from Gcn4 transcription factor to restore dimerization of the motor heads.
source: In Kip3ΔT-LZ, the putative cargo-binding tail was truncated and replaced with a leucine zipper domain from Gcn4 transcription factor to restore dimerization of the motor heads (Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the mutant construction.

claim: In kip3ΔT-LZ lysates, kinetochores still moved processively toward the plus end of microtubules.
source: Strikingly, in kip3ΔT-LZ lysates, kinetochores still moved processively toward the plus end of microtubules (Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Deleting the tail domain increased the velocity and the average run length of the kinetochore on the lattice of the microtubule.
source: In fact, deleting the tail domain increased the velocity and the average run length of the kinetochore on the lattice of the microtubule (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In Kip3+ versus kip3ΔT-LZ lysate, the laterally bound plus end velocity increased from 0.56 µm/min to 0.76 µm/min.
source: In Kip3 +versus kip3ΔT-LZ lysate, the laterally bound plus end velocity increased from 0.56 µm/min to 0.76 µm/min and the average run length increased from 0.56 µm/min to 1.4 µm/min (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In Kip3+ versus kip3ΔT-LZ lysate, the average run length increased from 0.56 µm/min to 1.4 µm/min.
source: In Kip3 +versus kip3ΔT-LZ lysate, the laterally bound plus end velocity increased from 0.56 µm/min to 0.76 µm/min and the average run length increased from 0.56 µm/min to 1.4 µm/min (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant protein did not accumulate on the plus ends of microtubules.
source: As previously reported, the Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant protein did not accumulate on the plus ends of microtubules and it was unable to destabilize their plus ends and cause depolymerization (Su et al., 2011; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and supported by a citation.

claim: The Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant protein was unable to destabilize microtubule plus ends and cause depolymerization.
source: As previously reported, the Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant protein did not accumulate on the plus ends of microtubules and it was unable to destabilize their plus ends and cause depolymerization (Su et al., 2011; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and supported by a citation.

claim: In a kip3Δ lysate, there was altered microtubule dynamics, specifically a diminished catastrophe frequency.
source: Similarly, in a kip3Δ lysate, there was also altered microtubule dynamics, specifically a diminished catastrophe frequency (Bergman et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and supported by a citation.

claim: In kip3ΔT-LZ lysates the kinetochore rarely reached the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules, despite its faster velocity.
source: Because of the reduced microtubule catastrophe frequency, we observed that in kip3ΔT-LZ lysates the kinetochore rarely reached the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules, despite its faster velocity.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Only 12.4% of kinetochores made it to microtubule plus ends in kip3ΔT-LZ lysates, compared to 28.1% in Kip3+ lysates.
source: Moreover, compared to the Kip3 +lysates wherein 28.1% of kinetochores completed travel to the microtubule plus end, only 12.4% of kinetochores made it to microtubule plus ends in kip3ΔT-LZ lysates.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The Kip3 tail domain is not required for kinetochore movement along microtubules, but it is required for kinetochores to reach the plus end.
source: These results indicate that the Kip3 tail domain is not required for kinetochore movement along microtubules, but it is required for kinetochores to reach the plus end.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations with the Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant.

claim: Kip3's dual functions are: (1) attenuating microtubule growth and (2) enabling movement of kinetochores processively on the lattice to allow end-on attachments to be made.
source: We conclude that Kip3's dual functions are: (1) attenuating microtubule growth and (2) enabling movement of kinetochores processively on the lattice to allow end-on attachments to be made (see Discussion).
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations with different Kip3 mutants.

claim: The assay allows individual kinetochores to be visualized while they are interacting with single microtubules.
source: We demonstrate that this assay allows individual kinetochores to be visualized while they are interacting with single microtubules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Kinetochores move to the microtubule plus ends powered by the budding yeast kinesin-8, Kip3.
source: We propose a model wherein kinetochores move to the microtubule plus ends powered by the budding yeast kinesin-8, Kip3.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: When kinetochores reach the microtubule plus ends, their attachments are converted to end-on attachments, at which point microtubule disassembly ensues.
source: When kinetochores reach the microtubule plus ends, their attachments are converted to end-on attachments, at which point microtubule disassembly ensues (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and summarized in the model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Kinetochore particles that contain multiple subunits from different subcomplexes were observed in the assay.
source: The common behavior of these kinetochore proteins, combined with their colocalization with each other (Figure 2), indicated that kinetochore particles that contain multiple subunits from different subcomplexes were observed in the assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The lysates retain the relative physiological concentration and ratio of soluble proteins.
source: Since our assay does not involve biochemical fractionation steps, and since the lysates retain the relative physiological concentration and ratio of soluble proteins, we were able to preserve the natural kinetochore composition (Biggins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of the whole cell lysate preparation and supported by a citation.

claim: The structures of kinetochores observed by cryo-correlative light-microscopy and electron tomography closely resemble negatively stained yeast kinetochores observed in earlier studies.
source: Most importantly, by using cryo-correlative light-microscopy and electron tomography, we were able to directly visualize kinetochores bound to both the sides and ends of microtubules and found that their structures closely resemble negatively stained yeast kinetochores observed in earlier studies (Gonen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the cryo-ET structures to previously published structures.

claim: Kinetochores that bind to the side of the microtubule lattice move processively towards the plus end.
source: Kinetochores that bind to the side of the microtubule lattice move processively towards the plus end.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Upon reaching the microtubule end, kinetochores convert their attachment to an end-bound conformation.
source: Upon reaching the microtubule end, kinetochores convert their attachment to an end-bound conformation.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: During their conversion from lateral- to end-on attachment, and while bound to the microtubule end, kinetochores remain stably attached to the microtubule.
source: During their conversion from lateral- to end-on attachment, and while bound to the microtubule end, kinetochores remain stably attached to the microtubule.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Once bound to the microtubule ends, kinetochores track the tip of the depolymerizing microtubule.
source: Once bound to the microtubule ends, kinetochores track the tip of the depolymerizing microtubule.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The transition to stable end-on attachments appeared to block microtubule polymerization and to induce depolymerization at a rate slower than the catastrophe rate for microtubules lacking kinetochores.
source: This transition to stable end-on attachments appeared to block microtubule polymerization and to induce depolymerization at a rate slower than the catastrophe rate for microtubules lacking kinetochores (Bergman et al., 2018, Figure 1a–e).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1 and compared to a prior study.

claim: In the presumably tension-less system, there was no observable kinetochore detachment from microtubule plus ends.
source: While tension stabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachments on dynamic microtubules (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), in our presumably tension-less system, there was no observable kinetochore detachment from microtubule plus ends.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and compared to prior literature.

claim: End-bound kinetochores do not normally detach from microtubules in vivo after attachment has been established during S phase.
source: Notably, end-bound kinetochores do not normally detach from microtubules in vivo after attachment has been established during S phase (Tanaka et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In a previous in vitro study, chromosomes remained stably associated with depolymerizing microtubule ends.
source: Additionally, in a previous in vitro study, chromosomes remained stably associated with depolymerizing microtubule ends (Koshland et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Reconstituted intact kinetochores associated with the lateral surface of dynamic microtubules stably, and they moved exclusively toward the plus end, and in a processive and kinesin-8-dependent manner.
source: Strikingly, reconstituted intact kinetochores associated with the lateral surface of dynamic microtubules stably, and they moved exclusively toward the plus end, and in a processive and kinesin-8-dependent manner.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In vivo, chromosomes binding to the lateral surface of microtubules move exclusively towards the minus-end in a Kar3-dependent manner.
source: This behavior contrasts with the in vivo observation of chromosomes binding to the lateral surface of microtubules and moving exclusively towards the minus-end in a Kar3-dependent manner (Tanaka et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, dynein has been reported to transport chromosomes captured by astral microtubules toward the centrosome.
source: In mammalian cells, dynein has been reported to transport chromosomes captured by astral microtubules toward the centrosome, while CENP-E is implicated in moving laterally bound chromosomes in the plus end direction toward the spindle equator to promote amphitelic sister kinetochore attachment (Maiato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, CENP-E is implicated in moving laterally bound chromosomes in the plus end direction toward the spindle equator to promote amphitelic sister kinetochore attachment.
source: In mammalian cells, dynein has been reported to transport chromosomes captured by astral microtubules toward the centrosome, while CENP-E is implicated in moving laterally bound chromosomes in the plus end direction toward the spindle equator to promote amphitelic sister kinetochore attachment (Maiato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In yeast, minus-end-directed Kar3 may transport chromosomes toward the spindle pole, while Kip3 moves chromosomes toward the equator.
source: We propose that in yeast, minus-end-directed Kar3 may transport chromosomes toward the spindle pole, while Kip3 moves chromosomes toward the equator.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations and comparison to mammalian systems.

claim: In the assay, kinetochores reached the plus end via a combination of directed movement and microtubule catastrophe.
source: In our assay, kinetochores reached the plus end via a combination of directed movement and microtubule catastrophe.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: A role for Kip3 in the translocation of kinetochores along microtubules is consistent with Kip3's reported in vivo colocalization with kinetochores.
source: A role for Kip3, the budding yeast kinesin-8, in the translocation of kinetochores along microtubules is consistent with Kip3's reported in vivo colocalization with kinetochores and with its Ndc10-dependent association with centromeric DNA in ChIP assays (Tytell and Sorger, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by a citation.

claim: A role for Kip3 in the translocation of kinetochores along microtubules is consistent with its Ndc10-dependent association with centromeric DNA in ChIP assays.
source: A role for Kip3, the budding yeast kinesin-8, in the translocation of kinetochores along microtubules is consistent with Kip3's reported in vivo colocalization with kinetochores and with its Ndc10-dependent association with centromeric DNA in ChIP assays (Tytell and Sorger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Quantification of kinetochore velocity on the microtubule lattice showed a wide distribution of rates punctuated by frequent pausing.
source: Additionally, quantification of kinetochore velocity on the microtubule lattice showed a wide distribution of rates punctuated by frequent pausing (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 1d-e.

claim: Kip3 affects kinetochore mobility in a stochastic way, perhaps by binding transiently.
source: Both of these observations lend themselves to a model in which Kip3 affects kinetochore mobility in a stochastic way, perhaps by binding transiently.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: The plus-end directed kinetochore motility observed is specifically dependent on a processive Kip3 motor and was not dependent on this kinesin's tail domain.
source: The plus-end directed kinetochore motility we observed is specifically dependent on a processive Kip3 motor and was not dependent on this kinesin's tail domain.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations with the Kip3ΔT-LZ mutant.

claim: Kip3 has a dual function in facilitating end-on attachment: (1) it induces microtubule catastrophe to allow kinetochores to catch up with elongating microtubule plus ends and (2) it moves kinetochores to the microtubule plus ends.
source: We propose that Kip3 has a dual function in facilitating end-on attachment: (1) it induces microtubule catastrophe to allow kinetochores to catch up with elongating microtubule plus ends and (2) it moves kinetochores to the microtubule plus ends.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations with different Kip3 mutants.

claim: In kip3Δ lysates, the inability to establish end-on attachments is likely largely due to a combination of impaired kinetochore motility and due to the microtubule dynamics being shifted toward more elongation with fewer catastrophes.
source: Specifically, in kip3Δ lysates, the inability to establish end-on attachments is likely largely due to a combination of impaired kinetochore motility and due to the microtubule dynamics being shifted toward more elongation with fewer catastrophes, making it less likely that kinetochores will reach microtubule plus ends (Figure 4a–d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In kip3ΔT-LZ lysates the kinetochores are highly motile, but they establish end-on attachments less frequently than in wild-type lysates.
source: In contrast, in kip3ΔT-LZ lysates the kinetochores are highly motile, but they establish end-on attachments less frequently than in wild-type lysates.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In kip3ΔT-LZ lysates, the catastrophe frequency is severely diminished compared to wild-type microtubule dynamics, and the microtubules mostly elongate faster than the rate of kinetochore translocation, so the kinetochores are less likely to encounter plus ends.
source: This result can be explained by the observations that the catastrophe frequency is severely diminished compared to wild-type microtubule dynamics, and that the microtubules mostly elongate faster than the rate of kinetochore translocation, so the kinetochores are less likely to encounter plus ends (Figure 5c–d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In wild-type cells, sister chromatids are clustered in two foci within the metaphase spindle.
source: In wild-type cells, sister chromatids are clustered in two foci within the metaphase spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about wild-type cell behavior.

claim: In kip3Δ cells metaphase kinetochores are declustered and aligned linearly along the spindle microtubules.
source: In contrast, in kip3Δ cells metaphase kinetochores are declustered and aligned linearly along the spindle microtubules.
evidence: This is observed in the in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The declustered kinetochore phenotype is also seen in kip3ΔT-LZ cells.
source: This declustered kinetochore phenotype is also seen in kip3ΔT-LZ cells (Tytell and Sorger, 2006; Wargacki et al., 2010; Su et al., 2011; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is observed in the in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5b and supported by citations.

claim: Laterally bound kinetochores are an intermediate on the pathway toward biorientation.
source: Based on the above in vitro and in vivo observations, we hypothesize that laterally bound kinetochores are an intermediate on the pathway toward biorientation, and that Kip3 is required for moving laterally attached kinetochores to the plus end of the microtubule during prometaphase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Kip3 is required for moving laterally attached kinetochores to the plus end of the microtubule during prometaphase.
source: Based on the above in vitro and in vivo observations, we hypothesize that laterally bound kinetochores are an intermediate on the pathway toward biorientation, and that Kip3 is required for moving laterally attached kinetochores to the plus end of the microtubule during prometaphase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: The previously reported declustered kinetochore phenotype is the result of an increased number of laterally bound kinetochores stalled all along spindle microtubules.
source: Specifically, we speculate that the previously reported declustered kinetochore phenotype is the result of an increased number of laterally bound kinetochores stalled all along spindle microtubules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.
